subject: One sided transect- how to address this in a detection function

messages.author: d87ed9174cc9d87b
messages.subject: One sided transect- how to address this in a detection function
parts:
Hello, 

 I am working with line transect data using the r package 'distance', where I am using perpendicular distances to clusters of animals. I am running into some issues as my 'N in covered region' is far larger than my density and abundance estimates and the model is telling me that the area my survey has covered in larger than my study area. I believe that this may be as a result of me using one sided transects. I am aware that using one-sided transects are not ideal for distance sampling, but is the only way that surveying is possible, as these data are being collected from a vehicle along a runway meaning that a full 360 view isn't possible. Is there a way to address this issue within the r package- i.e. tell it that each transect is only half the sampling effort when fitting the detection function? I currently have the sampling effort set to transect length- I have tried setting the effort to '0.5' but this does not seem to address the issue either. Is there something that I missing? 

Would greatly appreciate any help, 

Thanks, 
Sam

Sam

Thanks for acknowledging the challenges of one-sided transects.

Directly to your issue, use the function `dht2` in the Distance package.  It has an argument `sample_fraction` that does exactly what you want it to do.

There is an example of the use of `sample_fraction` in the new vignette we just posted for analysis of camera trapping data in a distance sampling context.  Of course cameras are a form of point transects, while you are doing line transects, but the concept is the same.  Have a look in the section labelled "Density estimates"

http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-cameratraps/camera-distill.html#density-estimates

messages.author: 7482eee8d2863d12
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] One sided transect- how to address this in a detection function
parts:
Sam,

In addition to Eric's response: I notice you said "these data are being
collected from a vehicle along a runway". I'm not sure exactly what
this means, but if you don't have random transect locations, then you
have issues to consider in addition to that of one-sided transects.
When transects not placed at random locations within the study area, then:

(a) the density on the transects is not necessarily representative of
that in the study area, so standard ("design-based") distance sampling
methods should not be used. Instead model-based methods (e.g., the DSM
engine) are needed to scale up from what's observed on the transects to
the study area. It may be that you are only interested in
density/abundance on the transects, so this is not an issue.

(b) the estimated detection function may be incorrect, and hence
estimates of density on the transect may be wrong. This occurs if there
is a density gradient in animals with respect to perpendicular distance
within the surveyed transects. For example, if the transects are on a
road and you are interested just in density on and close to the road, it
may be that there are almost no animals actually on the road, but then
increasing density for a few hundred meters as you go away from the
road. This means the pattern of detected distances does not tell you
about detectability alone - but is a mix of declining detectability and
increasing density. There are methods to deal with this (e.g., Marques
et al. 2010. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x ; also a
Mark recapture distance sampling) but they require special data
collection protocols. Another option is to do a set of transect
perpendicular to the roads to check how density varies in that direction
(and hopefully show it does not!).

You can find more discussion of these issues in previous postings to
this group (search for, e.g., "Roadside").

I hope this is helpful!

Len
